why: Every customer above a certain size already runs Kafka in some form (MSK, Confluent Cloud, Redpanda, Event Hubs) and expects your product to consume from their topics and publish back onto them under their schema registry, ACLs and retention rules; the FDE is the person who reads their topic contract, sizes the consumer group, and explains on a Friday night why the pilot dropped or duplicated events. Just as often the customer does not have Kafka and an architect on their side wants it for four hundred events a day, and the fastest way to earn credibility is a one-page memo showing a webhook or a Postgres table does the job with a tenth of the operational weight. The phrase 'exactly-once' will be said in a design review by someone holding a vendor slide; you need to state in one sentence exactly what it covers and design the idempotent consumer for everything it does not.
prerequisites: PostgreSQL from topic 29: transactions and isolation, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and enough about WAL to understand what `wal_level=logical` and a replication slot are
Redis from topic 31: `SET NX EX` idempotency keys and Redis Streams consumer groups (`XREADGROUP`/`XACK`), so you can compare a Stream to a Kafka partition honestly
FastAPI in production from topic 26: lifespan hooks for creating and flushing a producer, and how background workers are deployed separately from the API process
Docker internals from topic 5: Compose networking and why a broker's advertised address differs from its bind address; TCP and TLS basics from topic 2
Observability from topic 21: Prometheus scraping, Grafana panels and W3C `traceparent` context propagation, which you will carry through record headers
Python with confluent-kafka-python (librdkafka) installed, plus Docker with at least 4 GB free for a three-broker Redpanda cluster, Postgres and Debezium Connect

subtopics.name: Log, queue or webhook: the decision
subtopics.learn: Place the three on a table by what the receiver controls: a webhook is sender-push (receiver must be up, sender owns retries, no replay, ordering unspecified, each new consumer means another endpoint to register); a queue such as SQS or a Postgres table drained with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` is competing consumers with per-message ack and delete (visibility timeout, no fan-out without an extra layer, nothing to replay after ack); a Kafka topic is a durable, replayable log that any number of consumer groups read at their own pace with per-key ordering. Reach for a topic when at least two of these hold: more than one independent consumer needs the same events, you need replay or reprocessing from history, per-key ordering matters, or sustained throughput is thousands per second rather than hundreds per day. Be able to say out loud what Kafka costs you: no per-message ack or delete, no built-in delayed delivery or priority, and the operational weight of brokers, a schema registry and consumer-group hygiene.

subtopics.name: Partitions, offsets, segments and retention
subtopics.learn: A topic is N independent append-only logs; each record has a partition and a monotonic offset, and ordering exists only inside one partition. On disk a partition is a directory of segments (`segment.bytes`, `segment.ms`) with `.index` and `.timeindex` files; retention is enforced per closed segment by `retention.ms`/`retention.bytes` under `cleanup.policy=delete`, so a one-hour retention with a 1 GB active segment still keeps hours of data, or by compaction under `cleanup.policy=compact`. Partition count is a one-way door: you can add partitions (`kafka-topics.sh --alter --partitions`, `rpk topic add-partitions`) but never remove them, and adding them changes the key-to-partition mapping for every keyed producer. Size it as max(target MB/s divided by per-partition MB/s, the most consumer instances you will ever run) and know that each partition costs file handles, replication traffic and leader-election time on failover.

subtopics.name: Keys, partitioners and what 'ordered' really means
subtopics.learn: The default partitioner is `murmur2(key) mod numPartitions`; null keys use the sticky partitioner (KIP-480, strictly uniform since KIP-794), which fills one batch to a single partition then moves on, so null-keyed records have no ordering at all. Ordering holds only for records with the same key in one partition from one producer, and only when `enable.idempotence=true` or `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1` stops a retried batch leapfrogging a later one. Choose keys deliberately for DefenderMate: `document_id` orders one document's lifecycle, `tenant_id` orders everything for a tenant but pins a large tenant to one partition (hot key). Detect skew with per-partition end offsets from `rpk topic describe -p` or `kafka-get-offsets.sh --topic documents.v1`.

subtopics.name: Producer path: acks, idempotence, batching, timeouts
subtopics.learn: Trace `send()` through the record accumulator: `batch.size` and `linger.ms` decide when a batch flushes, `compression.type=lz4|zstd` compresses per batch, and a full `buffer.memory` blocks for `max.block.ms` then throws. `acks=0` is fire-and-forget, `acks=1` is leader-only (lost on leader failover), `acks=all` waits for the in-sync replicas. `enable.idempotence=true` (default since 3.0) assigns a producer id plus per-partition sequence numbers so the broker dedupes retries, and forces `acks=all`, `retries=MAX_INT` and in-flight at most 5; it does not survive a producer restart. `delivery.timeout.ms` (default 120 s) is the total budget including retries and must exceed `linger.ms + request.timeout.ms`. The delivery callback, not the return value of `send()`, is where you learn a record was lost, so in confluent-kafka-python always pass `on_delivery=` and call `flush()` on shutdown.

subtopics.name: Replication, ISR and the durability equation
subtopics.learn: Each partition has one leader and N-1 followers; the in-sync replica set (ISR) is the followers within `replica.lag.time.max.ms` of the leader, and the high watermark is the last offset replicated to the whole ISR, which is as far as consumers can read. `acks=all` waits for the ISR, and `min.insync.replicas` sets how small the ISR may shrink before writes fail with `NotEnoughReplicas` instead of quietly losing durability. RF=3 with `min.insync.replicas=2` and `acks=all` survives one broker; losing two makes the topic unwritable, which is the correct trade. `unclean.leader.election.enable=false` (default) chooses unavailability over electing an out-of-sync replica that truncates committed records. Spread replicas with `broker.rack`. Since 3.3 the controller quorum runs on KRaft (KIP-500) instead of ZooKeeper; Redpanda runs Raft per partition and has no separate controller tier.

subtopics.name: Consumer group protocol and rebalances
subtopics.learn: A group coordinator broker owns each group: members send JoinGroup and SyncGroup (classic protocol) and one member, the leader, runs the `partition.assignment.strategy` (Range, RoundRobin, StickyAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor). Eager strategies revoke every partition from every member on any change (stop-the-world); cooperative (KIP-429) revokes only the partitions that move, across two rounds. KIP-848 (`group.protocol=consumer`, GA in 4.0) moves assignment into the broker so rebalances are incremental and driven by per-member heartbeats. Know the triggers: member join or leave, `session.timeout.ms` expiring on missed heartbeats, `max.poll.interval.ms` expiring, a partition-count change, or subscription change. More consumers than partitions leaves consumers idle; `group.instance.id` (static membership) lets a restarted pod reclaim its partitions without a rebalance if it returns within `session.timeout.ms`.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Consumer Rebalance Protocol (KIP-848)

subtopics.name: The poll loop: heartbeats, max.poll.interval.ms and backpressure
subtopics.learn: Heartbeats run on a background thread every `heartbeat.interval.ms`, but `poll()` itself is the liveness signal for processing: fail to call it within `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 300 s) and the consumer leaves the group and its partitions are reassigned while you are still working, guaranteeing duplicates. Bound work per poll with `max.poll.records` (Java) or one-message-at-a-time in librdkafka, and for slow per-record work such as an LLM call per chunk use `pause()`/`resume()` on the partitions while a bounded worker pool drains, so `poll()` keeps being called. `fetch.min.bytes` and `fetch.max.wait.ms` trade latency for batch efficiency; `max.partition.fetch.bytes` must exceed your largest record or the consumer stalls on it forever. Implement `on_revoke` to commit or flush in-flight work before partitions move.

subtopics.name: Offsets: commit ordering, auto.offset.reset, expiry and lag
subtopics.learn: Committed offsets live in `__consumer_offsets` keyed by (group, topic, partition) and mean 'next offset to read'. `enable.auto.commit=true` commits the offsets returned by the previous `poll()` on the next `poll()` every `auto.commit.interval.ms`, so any handler that has not finished can be committed past; explicit commit-after-process gives at-least-once and commit-before-process gives at-most-once. `auto.offset.reset` applies only when the group has no committed offset or it is out of range: `latest` (default) silently skips all history for a brand-new group, `earliest` replays everything, `none` throws. Offsets for an empty group expire after `offsets.retention.minutes` (7 days), so a service down for eight days restarts as if new. Operate with `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group X` (CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET, LAG), `--reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-01-01T00:00:00.000 --execute` while the group is inactive, or `rpk group seek`. Lag per partition, not the total, is the SLI.

subtopics.name: Delivery semantics: what 'exactly-once' actually claims
subtopics.learn: Decompose the guarantee into three hops: producer to broker (the idempotent producer removes duplicates caused by retries), consumer position (commit placement decides duplicate versus loss), and the side effect (whatever your consumer does to the outside world). Kafka's exactly-once semantics cover only consume-transform-produce where inputs, outputs and offset commits are all inside Kafka and committed atomically in one transaction, read by consumers with `isolation.level=read_committed`. The moment a consumer writes to Postgres, calls an HTTP API or invokes a model, EOS ends and you need an idempotent consumer or a transactional outbox; practise saying that in one sentence to an architect who has read a vendor slide. Know that `read_committed` consumers cannot read past the last stable offset (LSO), so a hung transaction blocks the partition until `transaction.timeout.ms` expires.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Design: Message Delivery Semantics

subtopics.name: Transactions internals: transactional.id, epochs and zombie fencing
subtopics.learn: A transactional producer sets `transactional.id` and calls `init_transactions()`, which registers with the transaction coordinator (owner of a `__transaction_state` partition) and bumps the producer epoch, fencing any older instance with the same id so its next send fails with `ProducerFenced`. Then `begin_transaction()`, `produce()` to any partitions, `send_offsets_to_transaction(offsets, consumer_group_metadata)` to fold the consumer commit into the same transaction, and `commit_transaction()`, which writes control markers into every involved partition. The `transactional.id` must be stable per input partition set (Kafka Streams uses one per task) or fencing protects nothing, and thousands of ids load the coordinator. Cost: extra round trips per commit, end-to-end latency bounded by commit interval, and `transaction.timeout.ms` must stay below the broker's `transaction.max.timeout.ms` (15 min default).

subtopics.name: Idempotent consumers: dedupe keys and the processed-events table
subtopics.learn: Make every handler safe to run twice: derive an idempotency key from the event (an `event_id` header, or `topic-partition-offset` as a fallback), and in the same Postgres transaction as the business write run `INSERT INTO processed_events(event_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, skipping the work when zero rows were inserted; commit the Kafka offset only after that transaction commits. For state updates prefer natural idempotence, an upsert such as `ON CONFLICT (document_id) DO UPDATE ... WHERE EXCLUDED.version > documents.version`, over a dedupe table. For side effects you do not own (a customer's REST API, email) pass the key through as an `Idempotency-Key` header and persist the response. A Redis `SET NX EX` check (topic 31) is faster but not atomic with the database write; know when that gap is acceptable and when it is not.

subtopics.name: Transactional outbox and CDC with Debezium
subtopics.learn: Dual writes (commit the row, then produce) lose or orphan an event whenever the process dies between the two; the fix is an `outbox` table written in the same transaction as the business row and relayed to Kafka by a separate process. Relay options: a poller (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, delete after the delivery callback; simple, but adds polling latency and load) or change data capture, where Debezium reads the Postgres WAL through a logical replication slot (`wal_level=logical`, `pgoutput` plugin, `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` if you need old values on updates) and the outbox event router SMT turns each row into a record on a topic derived from `aggregatetype`, keyed by `aggregateid`. Understand slot risk: an idle slot pins WAL forever and fills the disk, so alert on `pg_replication_slots` lag. CDC is at-least-once, so the consumer side still needs the idempotency work from the previous subtopic.

subtopics.name: Schemas: registry, wire format and compatibility modes
subtopics.learn: Serialise with Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema through a schema registry; the Confluent wire format prefixes each payload with a magic byte and a 4-byte schema id, so consumers fetch the writer schema by id and resolve it against their reader schema. Set subject compatibility deliberately: BACKWARD (default; new schema reads old data, so consumers upgrade first, and you may only delete fields or add fields with defaults), FORWARD (producers upgrade first), FULL, and the `_TRANSITIVE` variants that check against every prior version rather than only the latest. Subject naming (`TopicNameStrategy` default versus `RecordNameStrategy` when many event types share one topic) decides what 'compatible' is checked against. JSON without a registry is a promise, not a contract, and renaming a field is always two releases: add the new field with a default, remove the old one later.

subtopics.name: Event design: notification vs state transfer, envelopes and PII
subtopics.learn: Decide per event type whether it is a thin notification (`document.uploaded {document_id}`; consumers call back for state and are coupled to your API's availability) or event-carried state transfer (the full document metadata rides along; consumers are decoupled but you have now published PII onto a retained log). Standardise the envelope on CloudEvents attributes (`id`, `source`, `type`, `time`, `subject`, `datacontenttype`), carried as Kafka headers in binary mode or as the JSON body in structured mode, and version the type name (`defendermate.document.uploaded.v1`). Never put PII in keys or headers: they survive compaction and show up in every console. For regulated customers pair state transfer with crypto-shredding, encrypting payload fields with a per-tenant key so erasure means deleting a key rather than rewriting an immutable log.

subtopics.name: Log compaction and tombstones for state topics
subtopics.learn: `cleanup.policy=compact` keeps the latest record per key rather than a time window, turning a topic into a durable changelog that a new consumer can bootstrap from with `auto.offset.reset=earliest` and end up holding current state for every key. Deletes are tombstones, a record with the key and a null value, retained for `delete.retention.ms` (24 h default) so lagging consumers see the delete before it is compacted away. Compaction runs only on closed segments and is governed by `min.cleanable.dirty.ratio`, `min.compaction.lag.ms` and `max.compaction.lag.ms`; the active head is never compacted, so 'one record per key' is a guarantee only after the cleaner catches up. Use `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` when you want both a key snapshot and an age bound.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Design: Log Compaction

subtopics.name: Failure handling: retries, dead-letter topics, poison pills
subtopics.learn: Separate transient from permanent failures in the handler: retry transient ones in-process with bounded exponential backoff while keeping `poll()` alive (pause the partition), and route permanent ones (deserialisation error, schema violation, business-rule rejection) to `<topic>.dlq` carrying the original bytes plus headers for exception class, message, source topic/partition/offset and attempt count, then commit and move on. A record the deserialiser throws on will otherwise crash-loop the consumer at the same offset indefinitely, so deserialise inside a try or use an error-handling deserialiser wrapper. Retry topics (`<topic>.retry.1m`, `<topic>.retry.10m`) trade per-key ordering for throughput; say so explicitly when you choose them. Kafka Connect exposes the same knobs as `errors.tolerance=all`, `errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name` and `errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable=true`. Build the replay path out of the DLQ before you need it.

resource.label: Confluent Developer - Event Streaming Patterns: Dead Letter Stream

subtopics.name: Observability: lag, broker health and trace propagation
subtopics.learn: Alert on consumer lag per partition and on its derivative (lag rising while produce rate is flat means a stuck consumer, not a busy one), exported by kafka-lag-exporter or Burrow, and on broker signals `UnderReplicatedPartitions`, `OfflinePartitionsCount`, `ActiveControllerCount != 1`, `RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent` and disk headroom. Propagate W3C `traceparent` through record headers so a trace spans producer, broker hop and consumer; follow the OpenTelemetry messaging semantic conventions (`messaging.system=kafka`, `messaging.destination.name`, `messaging.kafka.message.key`, `messaging.kafka.offset`, `messaging.consumer.group.name`) and model consumption as a `receive` span plus a `process` span per record with span links, because one poll can carry records from many producer traces. Log (topic, partition, offset, key) on every handler error so support can replay one record instead of a day.

subtopics.name: Security and multi-tenant isolation on a shared cluster
subtopics.learn: Authenticate clients with SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512 or mTLS on a TLS listener (`security.protocol=SASL_SSL`, `sasl.mechanism=SCRAM-SHA-512`) and authorise with ACLs: `kafka-acls.sh --add --allow-principal User:ingest --operation Write --topic documents.v1`, `--operation Read --group ingest-workers` for the consumer group, and `--resource-pattern-type prefixed` to cover `tenant-a.*`. Once `authorizer.class.name` is set, a resource with no ACL is denied unless `allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true`, which you should never ship. Protect tenants from each other with quotas (`producer_byte_rate`, `consumer_byte_rate`, `request_percentage` per user or client id via `kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config`) so one tenant's replay cannot starve the rest. Decide topic-per-tenant (hard, ACL-enforceable isolation; partitions and metadata scale linearly with tenants) versus a shared topic keyed by tenant (efficient; isolation exists only in your application code) and write the reasoning down.

subtopics.name: Lab: rebuild DefenderMate ingestion on a local Redpanda cluster
subtopics.learn: Run a three-broker Redpanda cluster with Docker Compose (`redpanda start --smp 1 --memory 1G --advertise-kafka-addr <node>:9092` per node) plus its built-in schema registry and console, create topics with `rpk topic create documents.v1 -p 6 -r 3 -c min.insync.replicas=2`, and rebuild the ingestion path as `document.uploaded` to chunker to `chunk.created` to embedder to `embedding.ready` using confluent-kafka-python with `acks=all`, `enable.idempotence=true`, manual commits after the Postgres write and the processed-events dedupe. Then break it on purpose: `docker kill` one broker mid-produce and compare lost-record counts under `acks=1` versus `acks=all`; SIGKILL the consumer between database commit and offset commit and count duplicates with and without the dedupe table; inject a malformed record and watch it land in the DLQ; watch lag with `rpk group describe`. Every assertion is a number printed by a script, not a screenshot.

outcomes: You can bring up a three-broker Redpanda cluster from Compose, create a topic with RF=3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`, produce 100k keyed records with `acks=all` and idempotence on, kill one broker mid-run and show zero loss and zero reordering per key; kill a second and show writes fail with `NotEnoughReplicas` rather than silently degrading.

You can demonstrate all three commit-placement outcomes (loss, duplicates, correct) by moving `commit()` before or after processing and SIGKILLing the consumer between them, then explain each outcome from the numbers in `rpk group describe` or `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe`.

You can run a consumer whose handler takes 90 seconds per record without it being evicted from the group, by pausing partitions and bounding work per poll, and show the rebalance log lines before and after the fix.

You can state in one sentence what Kafka's exactly-once semantics do and do not cover, then show a consume-transform-produce transaction where a `read_committed` consumer never sees the aborted records and a `read_uncommitted` one does.

You can implement outbox plus Debezium CDC into Redpanda and prove atomicity: kill the API between the Postgres commit and any produce call, and show the event still arrives and is processed exactly once downstream thanks to the processed-events table.

You can register an Avro schema, attempt a breaking change (removing a field without a default under BACKWARD compatibility), have the registry reject it with an HTTP 409, and show an old consumer still reading records written by a compatible new producer.

You can size a topic from a throughput target and consumer parallelism ceiling, explain why the count cannot shrink, and demonstrate what breaks for a keyed, stateful consumer when partitions are added.

You can hand a customer a one-page 'when not to Kafka' memo with a decision matrix across webhook, SQS, Postgres queue, Redis Streams and Kafka, each row backed by a concrete number (events/day, consumers, replay window, ordering need, ops headcount).
failureModes: A new consumer service shipped with the default `auto.offset.reset=latest`; because the group had no committed offset it skipped the entire backlog produced before its first deploy, and nobody noticed until a monthly reconciliation found 40,000 documents that were never embedded.

Each record triggered an LLM call with client-side retries, so a batch took longer than `max.poll.interval.ms`; the consumer was evicted, its partitions moved to a peer that reprocessed the same batch and was also evicted, producing a rebalance storm where lag climbed for hours while CPU sat near zero.

One malformed message from an upstream team made the deserialiser throw before `poll()` returned; the consumer crash-looped on the same offset for six hours and the fix (catch, publish to a DLQ with the offset in headers, commit) took ten minutes once someone looked at the offset in the logs.

Someone added partitions to a keyed topic to 'increase throughput'; murmur2 now mapped the same `document_id` to a different partition, the stateful downstream consumer saw updates out of order, and its last-write-wins logic reverted several documents to stale versions before anyone connected the two events.

A team turned on transactions and told the customer the pipeline was exactly-once, but the consumer also POSTed purchase orders to the customer's ERP; a rebalance re-delivered a batch and the ERP received duplicate orders, because Kafka transactions never covered the HTTP side effect.

A consumer group was offline for eight days during a migration, longer than `offsets.retention.minutes`; on restart the expired offsets fell back to `earliest`, replaying a week of events through a non-idempotent notification forwarder that sent every customer duplicate emails.

`advertised.listeners` was left pointing at `localhost:9092` inside Compose, so clients could connect for metadata but were redirected to an unreachable address; the producer hung and eventually failed with 'Local: Message timed out' and half a day was lost before anyone compared bind address to advertised address.
interviewQuestions: A customer's architect insists on Kafka for a pilot that ingests about 5,000 documents a day from a SaaS webhook into our product. Walk me through how you decide, what you propose instead if you disagree, how you make that case without losing the room, and what facts would change your mind.

Define exactly-once in Kafka precisely: which components participate, which configs enable it, and where the boundary of the guarantee sits. Then our consumer writes to Postgres and calls a third-party REST API for every event; design effectively-once end to end and name what is still not guaranteed.

Debug this: lag on a single partition grows without bound while other partitions are healthy, consumer CPU is low, and the logs show repeated 'Attempt to heartbeat failed since group is rebalancing'. Talk me through your hypotheses, what you check in what order, and the fix.

Design multi-tenant event ingestion for an AI product where tenants differ 100x in volume, per-document ordering matters, and one tenant's replay must never starve another. Topics per tenant or a shared topic keyed by tenant? Partition count, quotas, ACLs, and how the answer changes at 10 tenants versus 2,000.

A service writes an order row to Postgres and then publishes to Kafka. Sometimes there is a row and no event, sometimes an event and no row. Fix it, then compare the two relay implementations for the outbox (polling versus WAL-based CDC) on latency, load, failure modes and what happens when the relay is down for a day.

We need to add a field now and rename another field next quarter in an event schema consumed by four teams we do not control. Which compatibility mode do you set, what is the rollout order for producers and consumers, and what exactly breaks if you get the order wrong?

Configure a topic for durability at a customer who cannot lose a single event: replication factor, `min.insync.replicas`, `acks`, unclean leader election, rack placement. For each single- and double-broker failure, tell me precisely what the customer experiences and what, if anything, they lose.
proofOfWork: A public repository with a `make prove` target that runs six named, self-asserting chaos scenarios against a three-broker Redpanda cluster, Postgres 16 with `wal_level=logical`, Debezium Connect and the rebuilt DefenderMate ingestion consumers: (1) broker kill under `acks=1` versus `acks=all` with idempotence, printing lost and reordered record counts per key; (2) consumer SIGKILL between database commit and offset commit, printing duplicate counts with and without the processed-events table; (3) a 90-second handler under default versus tuned poll settings, printing whether the member was evicted; (4) a poison-pill record, asserting it lands in the DLQ with source topic, partition, offset and exception headers while the group keeps moving; (5) outbox atomicity, killing the API between commit and any produce call and asserting the event still arrives exactly once downstream; (6) a breaking Avro change rejected by the schema registry with a 409 while an old consumer keeps reading new records. Each scenario ends with PASS or FAIL against a numeric assertion, the run writes a results table into the README, and a Grafana dashboard JSON in the repo shows per-partition lag, under-replicated partitions and end-to-end trace latency during the run. Alongside it sits a two-page 'consuming from the customer's Kafka' runbook covering credentials, ACL requests, schema registry access, offset reset procedure and the questions to ask before the first connection.
